summary.summary: Wakefield's 2025/26 treasury outturn was fully compliant: the CFR rose £13.5m to £571.3m while external borrowing actually fell £3.1m to £377.9m (PWLB £346.4m, other local authorities £26.5m, banks £5m), leaving the council £131.9m under-borrowed and running on internal cash — capital slippage saved £4.2m of borrowing costs and the treasury budget underspent £3.85m. The average rate paid on external debt was 4.80%, and the council flags that the LA-to-LA borrowing market is 'becoming tight' as other authorities chase the same borrow-short-until-rates-fall strategy; investments stood at £57m (£40m in the DMO deposit facility, £17m lent to other councils). A legacy MRP overpayment that has been suppressing the revenue charge for debt is nearly exhausted — £5.3m left, fully used by end-2026/27, after which all MRP hits the revenue budget. Financing costs ran at 11.30% of net revenue (9.68% excluding PFI) against budgets of 13.16% and 9.70%.
summary.as_of_doc: Treasury Management for the year ending 31 March 2026.

signals.headline: £131.9m under-borrowed against the £571.3m CFR at 31 March 2026, on a deliberate short-term debt stance, while the council itself reports the LA-to-LA borrowing market 'becoming tight'
signals.why: The deferred borrowing need must eventually be financed externally, and the council's preferred market for short money is the one it says is tightening.

signals.headline: Legacy MRP overpayment offset down to £5.3m at 31 March 2026 and fully utilised by end-2026/27 — thereafter all MRP is charged to the revenue budget; the average rate paid on external borrowing was already 4.80% in 2025/26
signals.why: A structural step-up in the revenue cost of debt arrives from 2027/28, just as deferred borrowing may need to be externalised at current rates.

compliance.notes: Strong, professionally advised (Link) combined capital + treasury strategy: prudential indicators, a 10-year liability benchmark, MRP policy, borrowing strategy and creditworthiness/counterparty policy are all well developed, and every applicable core requirement scores >=2. Weakest areas are the non-treasury/commercial-investment framework (no explicit paras 51-53 compliance statement, no confirmed IMPs, no monetary limits on service/commercial investment, thin statutory disclosures, guarantees not reassessed), the absence of a quantitative investment-portfolio risk indicator (INV-06), accounts-linked reporting items not evidenced in the strategy (audit-qualification flag, financial-instruments disclosures), and ESG which is only referenced as a future Code requirement. Note: the documents contain no HRA content (housing stock transferred to WDH), so HRA-split and separate-HRA-benchmark elements are treated as not applicable.

news_drafts.headline: Wakefield cuts capital programme by £56m as spending lags and oversight remains incomplete
news_drafts.lead: Wakefield Council has reduced its five-year capital programme from £414.7m to £358.5m in the first quarter of 2026-27, with a further reprofiling planned within weeks. Capital spending in the first three months reached only £22m against a projected £138m quarterly rate, running at 15.9 per cent of profile. The revised programme relies on £140.2m of prudential borrowing (borrowing to fund long-lived assets), representing 39 per cent of total spending, but the council has provided no detailed assessment of how this will affect the revenue budget. The Cabinet papers acknowledge that governance arrangements for the capital programme are currently under review and do not yet fully embed the Duty of Best Value. A further reprofile and budget challenge will take place in the second quarter.

findings.paper_title: 22.09.26 10 point briefing Cabinet Report Disposal Programme
findings.headline: Governance changes remove barriers to property disposals, suggesting previous delays and new urgency.
findings.detail: The Scheme of Delegation is being amended to restrict ward members' ability to block or pause disposals. Previously any ward member objection could halt a disposal; the new approach allows objections only on 'legitimate grounds' for retention or alternatives. This suggests ward opposition has previously delayed key disposals.
findings.matters: It shows the council recognises disposal pace is critical to meeting budget targets and has removed a governance bottleneck, increasing credibility of programme delivery.
findings.quote: the Leader will amend the Scheme of Delegation to only permit such objections where legitimate grounds exist to support retention or an alternative to disposal

findings.paper_title: 22.09.26 10 point briefing Cabinet Report Disposal Programme
findings.headline: Property disposal programme is explicitly tied to meeting the council's essential revenue budget savings.
findings.detail: The council's Property, Facilities, Health & Safety service is using the disposal programme to meet essential revenue budget savings by reducing holding costs and generating capital receipts. This signals the council faces material property costs that are part of its budget challenge.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand councils' strategies for addressing budget pressures; identifying property costs as controllable allows assessment of the council's financial management approach and available levers.
findings.figures: No specific savings targets or capital receipt amounts provided.
findings.quote: This will allow the Council's Property, Facilities, Health & Safety service (PFHS) to meet essential revenue budget savings by reducing holding costs and generating capital receipts

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing requirement of £140.2m over five years to deliver £358.5m capital programme
findings.detail: The capital programme requires £140.2m of prudential borrowing over five years. The council's total gross borrowing at 30 June stood at £340m, comprising £333m from PWLB and £7m from inter-authority lending.
findings.matters: Shows the scale of additional borrowing committed and confirms funding is arranged through low-cost PWLB sources
findings.figures: £140.2m prudential borrowing; £358.5m total capital programme; £340m total gross borrowing
findings.quote: The revised capital programme requires £140.2m of prudential borrowing over the 5 years.

findings.headline: Capital spending in first quarter at only 15.9% of the annual £138m target, with further review planned
findings.detail: Of the £138m planned for 2026/27, only 15.9% was spent in the first quarter. The council acknowledges this slow delivery and states that review and challenge of planned spending will be undertaken in the next quarter.
findings.matters: Slower-than-expected capital delivery in early quarter indicates potential project delay risk that could affect funding drawdown timing and borrowing requirements
findings.quote: Of the £138m planned spend in 2026/27 only 15.9% was spent in the first quarter.

findings.headline: Council has secured £2,522,818 of additional CRSTS uplift funding from the Department for Transport for highways asset management in 2026/27.
findings.detail: This uplift funding from the West Yorkshire Combined Authority supplements the baseline CRSTS allocation for highways asset maintenance and improvements across the district. The funding supports the Council's statutory duty to maintain public highways under Section 41 of the Highways Act 1980. Cabinet is asked to accept the funding and approve its inclusion in the Council's Capital Programme.
findings.matters: Securing additional external capital funding beyond baseline allocations strengthens the council's financial position by reducing reliance on borrowing and demonstrates successful access to grant funding from higher-tier authorities.
findings.quote: The Council has secured £2,522,818 of additional capital funding from the Department for Transport via WYCA for highway asset management and maintenance during 2026/27.
